Prior to the founding of the University of Cambridge in 1209, [Cambridge](/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") and the area surrounding it already had developed a scholarly and ecclesiastical reputation largely due to the intellectual and academic contributions of monks from the nearby [Ely Cathedral](/wiki/Ely_Cathedral "Ely Cathedral"). The founding of the university, however, mostly originated with an incident at the [University of Oxford](/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") during which two Oxford scholars, following the death of a local woman, were [hanged](/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") by the town's secular authorities. The local ecclesiastical authorities, who were not consulted, would have traditionally been inclined to pardon scholars in such cases. During this time, Oxford's town authorities were in conflict with [King John](/wiki/John,_King_of_England "John, King of England"). Fearing more violence from Oxford townsfolk, University of Oxford scholars began leaving Oxford for more hospitable cities, including Paris, [Reading](/wiki/Reading,_Berkshire "Reading, Berkshire"), and [Cambridge](/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge"). Enough scholars ultimately took residence in Cambridge to form, along with the many scholars already there, the nucleus for the new university's formation.[[18]](#cite_note-Early_records-19)[[19]](#cite_note-20)[[20]](#cite_note-21)

By 1225, a chancellor of the university was appointed, and writs issued by [King Henry III](/wiki/Henry_III_of_England "Henry III of England") in 1231 established that rents in Cambridge were to be set *secundum consuetudinem universitatis*, according to the custom of the university, and established a panel of two masters and two townsmen to determine these. Milliken became Chancellor of the [City University of New York](/wiki/City_University_of_New_York "City University of New York") in 2014, and held the position through 2018.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

While at CUNY, Milliken was lauded for improving access to higher education and expanded an initiative called ASAP, or Accelerated Study in Associate Programs, that provided financial help, including free MetroCard fare, and tutors. CUNY's graduation rates climbed and gained national recognition for the ASAP program.[[16]](#cite_note-Najmabadi-16)

In November 2016, an interim report of an investigation conducted by the office of [New York State Inspector General](/wiki/New_York_State_Inspector_General "New York State Inspector General") found "financial waste and abuse", citing shoddy oversight and mismanagement that created a system ripe for financial waste and abuse, and criticized Milliken and CUNY General Counsel Frederick Schaffer, among others.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) The 2016 report was based on findings that pre-dated Milliken's time as chancellor of CUNY and a group of New York city council members suggested New York State Governor [Andrew Cuomo](/wiki/Andrew_Cuomo "Andrew Cuomo") was using the report to politicize the system.[[16]](#cite_note-Najmabadi-16) During the year preceding Milliken's resignation due to health concerns, Cuomo replaced CUNY Board of Trustees chairman [Benno C. Schmidt Jr.](/wiki/Benno_C._Schmidt_Jr. "Benno C. Schmidt Jr.") with a new chairman [Bill Thompson](/wiki/Bill_Thompson_(New_York_politician) "Bill Thompson (New York politician)"), and nearly all of the members of CUNY's board of trustees with a new politically prominent bloc.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

Whilst the association between alcohol abuse and [pancreatitis](/wiki/Pancreatitis "Pancreatitis") is well established the association between alcohol consumption and [pancreatic cancer](/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") is less clear. Overall the evidence suggests a slightly increased risk of pancreatic cancer with chronic heavy alcohol consumption but the evidence remains conflicting with a number of studies finding no association.,[[128]](#cite_note-Ye-128)[[129]](#cite_note-Silverman-129) but no increased risk for people consuming up to 30g of alcohol a day[[130]](#cite_note-Michaud-130)

Overall, the association is consistently weak and the majority of studies have found no association.[[31]](#cite_note-aa213-31)[[130]](#cite_note-Michaud-130)[[131]](#cite_note-131) Although drinking alcohol excessively is a major cause of [chronic pancreatitis](/wiki/Chronic_pancreatitis "Chronic pancreatitis"), which in turn predisposes to pancreatic cancer, chronic pancreatitis associated with alcohol consumption is less frequently a precursor for pancreatic cancer than other types of chronic pancreatitis.[[132]](#cite_note-cruk-132)

Some studies suggest a relationship,[[133]](#cite_note-133) the risk increasing with increasing amount of alcohol intake.[[134]](#cite_note-134)[[135]](#cite_note-135) The risk is greatest in heavy drinkers,[[128]](#cite_note-Ye-128)[[129]](#cite_note-Silverman-129)[[136]](#cite_note-136) mostly on the order of four or more drinks per day.[[137]](#cite_note-137) There appears to be no increased risk for people consuming up to 30g of alcohol a day,[[130]](#cite_note-Michaud-130)[[138]](#cite_note-138)[[139]](#cite_note-pmid=19258474-139) which is approximately 2 alcoholic beverages/day,[[139]](#cite_note-pmid=19258474-139) so most people who take alcohol do so at a level that "is probably not a risk factor for pancreatic cancer"

The Dodgers were founded in 1883 as the **Brooklyn Atlantics**, borrowing the name of a [defunct team](/wiki/Brooklyn_Atlantics "Brooklyn Atlantics") that had played in Brooklyn before them. The team joined the [American Association](/wiki/American_Association_(19th_century) "American Association (19th century)") in 1884 and won the AA championship in 1889 before joining the [National League](/wiki/National_League_(baseball) "National League (baseball)") in 1890. The team was known alternatively as the **Bridegrooms**,  **Grooms, Superbas, Robins** and **Trolley Dodgers**, before officially becoming the **Brooklyn Dodgers** in the 1930s.
